title: The One With The Giant Poking Device

jokes.text: See, that is the problem with invisible dentists. It's very unsettling to see all those metal tools just flying around.
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she can't see her dentist. Joey mishears or willfully misinterprets 'can't see him' as 'invisible dentist.'
jokes.punchline: Joey plays it completely straight, expressing concern about flying dental tools as if invisible dentists are a real and relatable problem.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey literalism. The joke works because Joey's deadpan extension of the misunderstanding ('very unsettling to see all those metal tools just flying around') adds vivid absurdist detail rather than just stopping at the misread. Strong character integration — this could only be Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't see my dentist anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, why not? Is he invisible?

jokes.text: That is so weird. Every time I go to the dentist... I look down the hygienist's blouse.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is about to reveal her strange dentist-related curse. Joey begins to mirror her phrasing, implying he has a similar weird experience.
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'weird thing' is simply ogling the hygienist — completely mundane and self-interested, deflating the supernatural buildup.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured misdirection. The parallel sentence structure ('Every time I go to the dentist...') primes the audience for another supernatural confession, then undercuts it with the most mundane possible Joey behavior. The economy is excellent — the punchline is nine words. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't go to my dentist.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because he's dead. He died last week, and I can't believe I'm the only one who cares. I was the only one at his funeral. Well, me and his family. But I didn't know them, so basically just me.

jokes.text: It's not about oral hygiene. I floss to save lives.
jokes.setup: The group is skeptical of Phoebe's curse connecting dentist visits to deaths.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reframes flossing as an act of heroism — she's not maintaining her teeth, she's preventing murders.
jokes.explanation: One of the tightest lines in the episode. Seven words that recontextualize oral hygiene as life-or-death heroism. Highly quotable, perfectly paced two-sentence structure, and quintessentially Phoebe — her sincere commitment to the absurd premise is exactly what makes her character work. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Every time I go to the dentist, I get a little excited.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because I know that afterwards, I can eat ice cream.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No wait, that's not it. Every time I go to the dentist, I think about this one time with my acting teacher, and I just...

jokes.text: It's just a coincidence. / Tell that to them. Oh, you can't! They're dead!
jokes.setup: Ross tries to dismiss Phoebe's curse as coincidence.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's comeback — 'Tell that to them. Oh, you can't! They're dead!' — uses the logical rebuttal to the rebuttal, delivered with genuine indignation.
jokes.explanation: The 'oh, you can't — they're dead!' structure is a classic comedy beat and it's executed well here. The escalation from rebuttal to self-interruption ('Oh, you can't!') gives it energy. Not totally original but the delivery context elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My dentist died. He was killed by my curse.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: First there was my mother's dentist, Dr. Waxler, he got bone cancer.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Then my dentist, Dr. Schulman, he had a stroke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Then my hygienist, Albino Bob, he got leukemia.

jokes.text: Thanks, Gunther. Can I get a napkin too? / Like you don't already have everything.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Gunther for a napkin at Central Perk, a simple, trivial request.
jokes.punchline: Gunther's bitter, jealous aside implies Rachel — who already has his heart — has no right to ask for more. The resentment is completely disproportionate to a napkin request.
jokes.explanation: Gunther's unrequited love for Rachel is a running gag across the series, and this is a solid, economical entry. The absurdity of his disproportionate bitterness over a napkin request is the engine of the joke. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I brush my teeth every day. I floss. I use mouthwash. It's basically like I'm performing surgery on my own mouth.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm like a dental superhero, saving lives one tooth at a time.

jokes.text: Fine. But if you're my next victim... don't come back as a poltergeist who sucks me into the TV set.
jokes.setup: The group pushes Phoebe to go to the dentist despite her fear of killing someone.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe accepts but adds a hilariously specific supernatural contingency — don't haunt me via the TV set.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'poltergeist who sucks me into the TV set' (a Poltergeist movie reference) is the joke's strength. Phoebe's supernatural worldview expressed through a very specific movie-logic fear is on-brand. Slightly overlong but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, no no no. I died in a previous life.

jokes.text: I promise. Although, don't feel like you can't visit.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks Ross not to haunt her as a poltergeist if she accidentally kills him.
jokes.punchline: Ross promises, but immediately hedges — as a ghost, he'd still be welcome to drop by. He's engaging with the supernatural premise completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: Nice quick button on the poltergeist bit. Ross playing along with the supernatural logic and then adding an open invitation is a sweet, funny beat. Economy is its strength.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Could I get a napkin?

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Oh, a napkin? Sure, why not? We have plenty of napkins. Some of us have been here since 6 AM making coffee for ungrateful people like you, but yes, let me just drop everything and get you a napkin. You're so welcome.

jokes.text: I think the best way would be... to not. / You can't keep this to yourself. If you know, you have to tell him. / It'll kill him. It'll just kill him. / Wait until I go to the dentist. Maybe I'll kill him.
jokes.setup: The gang debates how to tell Chandler that Janice was seen kissing her ex-husband.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe turns the tense ethical discussion into a callback to her dentist curse — she could just schedule an appointment and solve the problem.
jokes.explanation: Effective callback that also functions as dark comedy — Phoebe casually proposes murder-by-dentist as a solution to an emotional problem. The juxtaposition of the serious scene with the absurd callback lands well. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to the dentist. I know I have that thing where I can't go to the dentist, but I'm gonna go.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's great!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah. Although I have to say, I'm pretty nervous because I have this weird thing where I think that if I go to the dentist, my teeth will get stolen and he'll use them to make a denture for a witch in Peru.

jokes.text: Ugly Naked Guy's using his new hammock. It's like a Play-Doh fat factory.
jokes.setup: The group is in tense conversation about the Janice situation. Rachel looks out the window.
jokes.punchline: The non-sequitur Ugly Naked Guy observation — describing his hammock-squished fat as a Play-Doh factory — is both a tension-breaker and a vivid, disgusting image.
jokes.explanation: The 'Play-Doh fat factory' simile is genuinely creative — it evokes the exact visual of fat being squeezed through hammock netting in a perfectly absurd, kid's-toy metaphor. The non-sequitur timing as a tension-breaker adds to the impact. One of the better pure image jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, that's so nice! You know, I think a ghost would really add to the apartment's character. We could give it its own shelf in the bathroom!

jokes.text: I'm going to the dentist. So listen... just be on the lookout for anything that you could fall into... or that can fall on you... or... Or just look out!
jokes.setup: Phoebe is about to leave for the dentist and gives farewell safety warnings to her friends.
jokes.punchline: The warnings devolve from specific dangers to a completely unhelpful 'just look out!' — Phoebe's concern is genuine but her advice is useless.
jokes.explanation: Escalation that collapses to absurdity works well for Phoebe. The deterioration from specific advice to generic panic ('just look out!') is a good structural beat. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, you just gotta avoid her. Don't answer the phone, don't go to places she might be, just completely disappear.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not a strategy, that's what you do with all your girlfriends.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Exactly! And it works!

jokes.text: And I also just want to... I just want to tell you all that... [long pause, Phoebe appears unable to say goodbye, then leaves without completing the sentence]
jokes.setup: Phoebe attempts a final, heartfelt goodbye to her friends before going to the dentist, seemingly aware she may cause a death.
jokes.punchline: She can't finish the sentence. The comedy is in the implied melodrama of a dentist appointment treated as a farewell forever, punctuated by her inability to get the words out.
jokes.explanation: A visual/performance beat where the joke is Phoebe's over-the-top solemnity about a dentist appointment. Works more on screen than on paper; the humor depends heavily on Lisa Kudrow's performance.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I have a curse. I could kill him for you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, no!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? It works.

jokes.text: Some kids messed up the Homo sapien display. / What did they do? / They painted over the word 'sapien,' for one thing. / Then they rearranged the figures. Let's just leave it at that.
jokes.setup: Ross explains why he needs to go into work — a museum display was vandalized by kids.
jokes.punchline: The kids turned the Homo sapiens exhibit into something obscene — implied by 'they painted over the word sapien' (leaving 'Homo') and 'rearranged the figures' (too inappropriate to describe).
jokes.explanation: Excellent implied joke. The structure is confident — tell enough, let the audience's imagination do the rest, then confirm with 'let's just leave it at that.' Two-tiered joke (the word defacement + the rearranged figures) with escalating implication. Strong economy. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: That would be great! I just asked Monica... because I know how empty her life is.
jokes.setup: Rachel volunteers to babysit; Ross explains why he originally asked Monica.
jokes.punchline: Ross's explanation is a cutting jab at Monica's social life — implying she has nothing going on and therefore is the natural babysitting choice.
jokes.explanation: A decent brotherly dig at Monica. The 'empty life' line is slightly mean-spirited in a way that fits Ross's occasionally tone-deaf character. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, and be careful of the ice on the sidewalk. And don't accept candy from strangers. And watch out for low-flying aircraft.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? Just... be careful of everything. Assume everything is trying to kill you, because it probably is.

jokes.text: I got a science question. If the Homo sapiens were, in fact, 'homo' sapiens... is that why they're extinct?
jokes.setup: Ross's story about the museum vandalism has just established the 'Homo sapiens' word, which Joey is now processing.
jokes.punchline: Joey connects 'homo' sapiens to 'homo' (homophobic implication) and then wrongly concludes they're extinct — a double error that reveals total scientific illiteracy.
jokes.explanation: Joey stupidity joke with a double-layered error (misunderstanding 'homo' AND not knowing humans aren't extinct). The 'is that why they're extinct?' extension elevates it beyond a simple gay joke. Somewhat reliant on Joey's established dim persona rather than fresh writing. The 'Hey, I'm not judging' button is a nice cap.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna go now. I just want you all to know that I've loved you so much. You've been like family to me.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, where are you going?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't know. But I want to say goodbye while I still can.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I just have this feeling...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is she dying?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what's going on?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm moving to Connecticut.

jokes.text: Joey, Homo sapiens are people. / Hey, I'm not judging.
jokes.setup: Ross corrects Joey that Homo sapiens are people, not a separate extinct group.
jokes.punchline: Joey hears 'Homo sapiens are people' and interprets it as Ross defending gay people — and Joey chimes in with open-minded acceptance, completely missing the correction.
jokes.explanation: 'Hey, I'm not judging' is four words that do enormous work — it completes Joey's misunderstanding while adding his characteristic open-minded acceptance of something he's still misunderstanding. Economy is near-perfect. Classic Joey button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God! They put a little... they drew little...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? What did they do?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: They gave the Homo sapiens a little... a little penis!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, they are historically accurate.

jokes.text: Ben bumps his head during the airplane game. Monica and Rachel's panicked reaction — 'Oh, my God! Well, push it in! Push it in! / I cannot push it in!'
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel drop Ross's baby Ben while playing the airplane game. They discover a bump on his head.
jokes.punchline: Their solution is to physically push the bump back into his skull — a hilariously misguided and alarming first aid idea delivered in full panic.
jokes.explanation: The 'push it in!' panic is strong cringe comedy — the absurdity of the medical advice combined with the genuine alarm makes it funny. The escalating horror of two supposedly responsible adults is the comedic engine here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't... I can't talk about this.

jokes.text: The second Ross walks in... take him to your bedroom, and do whatever it is you do... that makes him go... [pause/implied sex noise]
jokes.setup: Monica devises a plan to distract Ross from noticing Ben's bump.
jokes.punchline: Monica suggests Rachel use sex to distract her own brother — catching herself mid-sentence as the full implication lands, before they pivot to 'or... we could put a hat on his head.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. The setup builds toward something clearly inappropriate (Monica suggesting Rachel use sex on Ross), the implied pause lets the audience catch up, and the hard pivot to 'or... we could put a hat on his head' is a perfect deflation. The discomfort of Monica almost suggesting her friend seduce her brother is genuinely funny cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I asked Monica to babysit because she's my sister and I trust her, but honestly, she has nothing else going on in her life anyway.

jokes.text: Or... we could put a hat on his head. / A hat! Yes! We need a hat! Where are we gonna find a tiny little hat?
jokes.setup: After nearly suggesting something inappropriate, Monica pivots to an alternative plan: cover Ben's bump with a hat.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately escalates into a crisis about WHERE to find a tiny hat, treating it as a massive logistical challenge.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of treating 'find a tiny hat' as an impossible quest is a solid escalation gag. Rachel's panic about the hat logistics is a good character beat — she's dramatizing a simple problem.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me that humans evolved from monkeys?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Not exactly from monkeys, Joey. We share a common ancestor.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right, right. So like, my great-great-great grandfather was a monkey?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not how evolution works.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How does it work then? 'Cause I'm pretty sure I'm not part monkey.

jokes.text: I'll get Rainy Day Bear! / Because he'll know what to do? / Oh, my God. You're a genius! / It's kind of sewn on.
jokes.setup: They need a tiny hat for Ben. Rachel announces she'll get Rainy Day Bear.
jokes.punchline: Monica's sarcastic 'Because he'll know what to do?' undercuts Rachel's confident plan. Then Rachel confirms she's after the bear's hat — which is sewn on, adding another obstacle.
jokes.explanation: Monica's sardonic 'Because he'll know what to do?' is a nice straight-man line. The added wrinkle of the hat being sewn on is a good escalation of their absurd predicament. Solid ensemble comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! I'm not prejudiced. I'm cool with it. I have... I have gay friends.

jokes.text: It's just like a bloodbath in here today! [Monica presumably referring to struggling with the sewn-on bear hat]
jokes.setup: Monica is fighting to remove the sewn-on hat from Rainy Day Bear — presumably producing some torn fabric or stuffing.
jokes.punchline: Monica dramatically calls it a 'bloodbath' — wildly overstating the carnage of attacking a stuffed animal.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual gag where the comedy is Monica's dramatic language applied to a trivial task. Functional but not especially clever.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, here we go, Ben. Airplane! Neeeeow!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wheeee!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Up, up, and away!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Monica, be careful!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, I've got this. I do this all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, Ben, here comes the landing. Whoa, whoa, whoa—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ow!

jokes.text: You wanna get her something special? Get her flowers. Get her candy. Get her gum. Girls love gum. / That's a good idea. 'Dear Janice: Have a Hubba Bubba birthday.'
jokes.setup: Chandler wants to buy Janice something special for her birthday. Joey offers advice, escalating from flowers to candy to gum.
jokes.punchline: Ross imagines the actual birthday card sentiment: 'Have a Hubba Bubba birthday' — reducing Chandler's romantic intentions to a gum-brand pun.
jokes.explanation: The 'Hubba Bubba birthday' punchline is a nice specific brand-name joke that works because the specificity ('Hubba Bubba' as a deliberate wordplay choice) elevates it above generic. The escalation from flowers to gum in Joey's gift advice is also funny in its descending thoughtfulness.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We have to tell Ross about the baby's injury.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? No! We could just... not tell him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, he's the father.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, but he doesn't have to know that we know that he knows... I mean, we could just not say anything and see if he notices.

jokes.text: You know what you should do? You should get her one of those... barium enemas. Those are dead serious. And you know she'll never get one for herself.
jokes.setup: Chandler says he wants a serious gift for Janice. Joey thinks hard and offers a recommendation.
jokes.punchline: Joey recommends a barium enema as a serious, thoughtful gift — and justifies it logically (she'd never treat herself). The medical specificity makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's gift logic is internally consistent and delivered with complete confidence — he has answered the brief ('serious') and even rationalized why it's a treat ('she'll never get one for herself'). This is Joey at his comedic peak: not just being dumb, but being dumb with airtight logic. 'Dead serious' is an inadvertent pun (barium enemas are associated with cancer screening). Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, there's a bump on the baby's head!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Where?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Right here! What do we do?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know, maybe we can just push it back in?

jokes.text: Bet that barium enema doesn't sound so bad now.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just learned that Janice kissed her ex-husband and is devastated.
jokes.punchline: Joey's callback to the barium enema gift suggestion — now reframed as merciful distraction from heartbreak — lands as dark comfort.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback economy — one sentence, timed perfectly after Chandler's heartbreak, recontextualizing the earlier absurd joke as darkly compassionate wisdom. The joke rewards attentive viewers. 'Doesn't sound so bad now' in the context of having your heart broken is genuinely funny and a little poignant.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I know! We could all go to that new restaurant that just opened up on Amsterdam!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, they have this really great... um... thing. You know, the kind of thing that Rachel and Ross do... a lot.

jokes.text: It makes more sense as an ensemble. Besides, it takes the focus off the hat. [Ross looking at Ben in the bear hat]
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel have dressed Ben in Rainy Day Bear's hat to hide his bump.
jokes.punchline: The visual of a baby in a stuffed animal hat is absurd. The joke acknowledges it by rationalizing the look as an 'ensemble' — fashion-forward deflection.
jokes.explanation: Relies on the visual (baby in bear hat) which is its strongest element. The 'ensemble' language is a nice Rachel-ism — fashionista vocabulary applied to baby disguise. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We could put a hat on the baby!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's... that's not how hats work. The bump is huge. You'd need a baby-sized hat.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So? We'll get a baby-sized hat!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: From where? The baby hat store? 'Excuse me, do you have anything in a 'suspicious bulge'?'

jokes.text: Oh! You're alive! You're alive!
jokes.setup: Phoebe returns from the dentist, relieved.
jokes.punchline: She greets her friends with the jubilation of someone who expected to cause a death — 'you're alive!' is both a greeting and a miracle.
jokes.explanation: Good callback. The relief in 'you're alive!' treats the dentist visit as genuinely life-or-death. Phoebe's commitment to the bit is the joke's engine.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You can borrow Mr. Fluffy!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, the bear is going to fix my relationship?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, you can use him to hold your hat.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh... I thought you meant he had emotional support powers or something.

jokes.text: I promised you no one would die, didn't I? / We'll see about that. Can I use your phone to call everyone I know?
jokes.setup: Phoebe is relieved no one died during her dentist visit.
jokes.punchline: She immediately undermines her own relief — 'we'll see about that' — and asks to call everyone she knows to verify they're alive.
jokes.explanation: The 'we'll see about that' is a wonderfully dark subversion — she expects the death toll to come in eventually. Asking to use the phone to do a mass welfare check is a great extension of the bit. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you guys, the most amazing thing just happened at the dentist. He was drilling, and the drill broke, and a piece of it flew across the room and hit him right in the eye. He's probably gonna lose his sight in that eye.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's horrible!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! And then when he was reeling back in pain, he fell into his tray table, and all his instruments went flying. One of them went right into his shoulder. There was blood everywhere!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's my curse. I'm like a black widow, but for dentists.

jokes.text: Hey, you're not dead! Okay, see you.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is on the phone calling everyone she knows to confirm they're alive.
jokes.punchline: We hear only one side of a call — a perfunctory 'not dead, great, bye' — capturing the absurd ritual in its most efficient form.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. The entire welfare call compressed to six words: 'Hey, you're not dead! Okay, see you.' We can imagine the confused person on the other end. The abruptness of 'Okay, see you' is perfectly Phoebe — mission accomplished, no social niceties needed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You gotta get her something nice. Women love getting gifts.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, like a card that says, 'I got you this gift because I have no idea who you are.'

jokes.text: Monica. / Oh, my God! He just said my name! / Monica bang!
jokes.setup: Ben (the baby) says Monica's name for the first time. Monica is thrilled.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately follows 'Monica' with 'bang' — a two-word phrase that reveals he associates Monica with something hitting his head.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a legitimate standout. The setup is innocent — baby says a name, adults are delighted — and the punchline is devastating: 'bang.' Two syllables that implicate Monica, delight the audience, and terrify the characters. The callback precision (Ben associates Monica with head trauma) is exceptional. Structure is close to perfect: joy, then horror. Approaches 8.0+ anchor territory. Highly quotable in context.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, if you really wanna impress her, you gotta get her something she really wants but would never buy for herself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, what are you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A boob job.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm serious! Chicks love that stuff.

jokes.text: Sweetie, you need to stop saying that now. / It's no big deal. It's not even worth mentioning. / You see? We all do it all the time. See? Watch this. Monica bang! Everybody bang! Ben bang! Rachel bang! Bang, Rachel! Bang!
jokes.setup: Ben keeps saying 'Monica bang,' threatening to expose what happened. Monica tries to normalize it.
jokes.punchline: Monica's attempt to normalize 'Monica bang' by having Rachel join in escalates into frantic, desperate chanting — the cover-up becoming more suspicious than the crime.
jokes.explanation: Escalating cringe comedy at its best. The attempt to normalize the damning phrase spirals into increasingly manic chanting. 'Ben bang! Rachel bang! Bang, Rachel! Bang!' is the sound of a cover-up collapsing in real time. Very well-structured escalation arc.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Think about it! It's practical, it's thorough, and it shows you really care about someone's health. Plus, it's something they'll never forget!

jokes.text: Yeah. You know, if it's not a headboard, it's just not worth it.
jokes.setup: After the 'Monica bang' chanting, the scene settles. Rachel comments on what it would take to make banging your head worthwhile.
jokes.punchline: Rachel delivers a dry TMI revelation — she's apparently only interested in head-banging incidents if they involve vigorous sex against a headboard.
jokes.explanation: A terrific button on the Monica bang sequence. The sexual implication delivered completely deadpan, with the further specificity of 'headboard,' is both character-consistent for Rachel and a genuinely funny line. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No no no no no, Chandler, no! You can't buy those pearls!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No no no no no!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No! No! No!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No...

jokes.text: Why are your eyes so wide?
jokes.setup: Chandler confronts Janice about the kiss, but she doesn't know he knows yet. She enters and notices something is off about Chandler's face.
jokes.punchline: Janice's innocent question about Chandler's wide eyes is the inadvertent reveal that he's holding back a devastating secret — the audience knows exactly why his eyes are wide.
jokes.explanation: A cringe-comedy beat — the dramatic irony of Janice asking why Chandler looks panicked while the audience knows he just learned she cheated. More tension than laugh, but it functions as an uncomfortable humor beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's having an affair? With who?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Some guy named Sid.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Sid? What kind of name is Sid? I suggested a nice Walkman!

jokes.text: You tell me. / Maybe it's because I was just fooling around with my ex. / Oh, no. That was you!
jokes.setup: Chandler deflects Janice's question about his wide eyes. Janice flippantly suggests it's because of someone fooling around.
jokes.punchline: Janice accidentally describes her own crime as a hypothetical — not realizing Chandler knows. 'Oh, no. That was you!' snaps the irony into focus.
jokes.explanation: Strong dramatic irony joke. Janice using 'fooling around with my ex' as a hypothetical when it's exactly what she did is well-constructed cringe. Chandler's 'Oh, no. That was you!' functions as both comedic revelation and emotional gut-punch.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, what else did you add to the costume?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A tiara? And a sash? And a wand? It's a baby, not a beauty pageant contestant!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I designed this to be a simple, cute outfit. Now it looks like a tiny Vegas showgirl.

jokes.text: I can't breathe. Can you get me a bag or something? / Here. Here. Here. [Chandler hands Janice the shopping bag / receipt moment]
jokes.setup: Janice is hyperventilating after being confronted about the kiss.
jokes.punchline: Chandler hands her a bag to breathe into — and then we learn it was the receipt from the pearls he almost bought her, a physically small/funny object for such an emotional moment.
jokes.explanation: Modest visual gag — the comedy of using a receipt as an impromptu hyperventilation bag. The irony of the birthday present receipt appearing in a breakup scene adds a layer. Somewhat undercut by the emotional weight of the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God! You're all still alive!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I went to the dentist today, and I know what that means. I thought for sure the death curse would've taken at least one of you by now.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You go to the dentist, someone dies. It's like a rule.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not a rule.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, it's SUPPOSED to be! I'm genuinely shocked right now.

jokes.text: It's the receipt. / I'll take it.
jokes.setup: Janice was breathing into what turns out to be a receipt. Chandler identifies it.
jokes.punchline: Janice says 'I'll take it' — either accepting the useless receipt or darkly acknowledging she'll take whatever she can get at this point.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient button. 'I'll take it' works on two levels (accepting the receipt; resigned acceptance of her situation) though the double meaning may not fully land. Economy is its strength.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Mommy pushed me down the stairs.

jokes.text: Okay, if you're alive, you answer your phone! [Phoebe yelling at an unanswered call]
jokes.setup: Phoebe is calling everyone she knows to confirm they're alive post-dentist.
jokes.punchline: Someone doesn't answer, and Phoebe interprets it as confirmation of death — 'if you're alive, you answer your phone!'
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's logic — unanswered phone = death — is perfectly consistent with her character's supernatural worldview. The line is declarative, funny, and quotable. Strong character integration. The exasperation in 'you answer your phone!' elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, we just need to say it naturally. Like it's a normal word.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Right, totally normal. Bang. See? Bang.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: BANG! It's just a word, people!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why are we all yelling 'bang'?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because we're normalizing it! BANG BANG BANG!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You guys sound completely unhinged right now.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do I? Do I sound unhinged? Is that what you're saying about me?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A little bit, yeah.

jokes.text: Okay, Ben, I won't tell your daddy that you had ice cream before dinner... if you won't tell him about our little bonking incident.
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to bribe Ben the baby into silence about the head bump.
jokes.punchline: Monica is negotiating with a baby using a quid pro quo — bribing him with ice cream cover to buy his silence, treating him as a fully rational co-conspirator.
jokes.explanation: Funny premise: bribing an infant. Monica's serious tone while conducting a conspiracy negotiation with a baby is well-played. The word 'bonking' has gentle innuendo bonus that makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I like it when a guy takes charge in bed.

jokes.text: Number one, I don't think Ben understands the concept of bribery. And number two, I... / What? / You said, 'number two.' / I also said, 'number one.' / I know.
jokes.setup: Rachel begins to explain why Monica's baby bribery won't work, using 'number one' and 'number two.'
jokes.punchline: Monica and Rachel both catch the potty-humor double meaning of 'number one' and 'number two' and dissolve into giggles, completely abandoning the serious point Rachel was making.
jokes.explanation: Classic potty-humor gag that plays on 'number one/number two' slang. It's charming because both adult women dissolve into giggles over a baby joke — which is somewhat character-appropriate given the baby context. But the wordplay itself is ancient and requires no craft. The meta-awareness ('I also said number one. / I know.') saves it slightly.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Hi Chandler! Oh. My. God.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more of a Bing?

jokes.text: How's my little boy? / He's perfect. Aren't you, Ben? / He's never been better. / What did you do, take him whaling?
jokes.setup: Ross returns to pick up Ben, who is wearing a tiny hat. Monica and Rachel insist everything is fine.
jokes.punchline: Ross, seeing Ben in the ridiculous hat, sarcastically asks if they took him whaling — implying Ben looks like a tiny sea captain.
jokes.explanation: 'What did you do, take him whaling?' is a vivid, specific image that perfectly captures the absurdity of a baby in a nautical-looking bear hat. The whaling reference is both unexpected and specific — it paints a scene. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you've never... you know... been with anyone else?

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh, well, there was that time in Aruba...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: ARUBA?!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: And then there was my yoga instructor, but that was just once.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: JUST once?! Janice!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh, and my dentist. But he was very gentle.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your DENTIST?!

jokes.text: Monica bang! / That's right. That's what I'd sound like if I exploded.
jokes.setup: Ben says 'Monica bang!' in front of Ross. Rachel needs to explain it away.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's improvised explanation — 'that's what I'd sound like if I exploded' — is completely nonsensical as cover but delivered with absolute confidence.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Rachel's cover story — 'that's what I'd sound like if I exploded' — is so confidently absurd that it almost sounds plausible. The deadpan delivery of a completely bonkers explanation is the joke. 'Monica bang' as an explosion sound effect is the kind of creative nonsense that becomes quotable. One of the episode's better lines.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're telling me there are multiple locations?

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Well, yeah! There's the main office, the warehouse, and the satellite branch.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Multiple locations? How many are we talking here?

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I don't know, like five or six?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Five or six?! That's not a business, that's a empire! I can't handle an empire! I can barely handle my apartment!

jokes.text: The curse is broken! I called everybody I know... and everyone is alive!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has completed her post-dentist welfare calls.
jokes.punchline: She triumphantly announces the curse is broken — celebrating the fact that no one died as a major personal victory.
jokes.explanation: A solid payoff beat for the dentist arc. Phoebe's genuine triumph at 'everyone is alive' is a good character moment. Sets up the immediate deflation of the Ugly Naked Guy beat perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, oh God, oh God!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: That's my receipt.

jokes.text: Ugly Naked Guy looks awfully still.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just announced the curse is broken and everyone is alive.
jokes.punchline: Immediately: Ugly Naked Guy appears to be dead. The curse strikes again within seconds of her declaration.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect comedic timing. The immediate juxtaposition of 'the curse is broken, everyone is alive!' followed by 'Ugly Naked Guy looks awfully still' is a masterclass in comic setup and instant payoff. The structure is essentially a joke where the setup IS the previous joke's punchline, creating a cascade. One of the episode's best moments. Economy: five words deliver the entire devastating irony.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, that plan doesn't make any logical sense. You're ignoring the basic financial implications, and frankly, the whole thing falls apart if you just think about it for five seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so what you're saying is... my plan is going down the toilet?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not what I— Monica, I'm being serious.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Number two serious, or number one serious?

jokes.text: My God, I killed another one! The curse is getting stronger too, to bring down something that big.
jokes.setup: Ugly Naked Guy appears motionless. Phoebe believes her curse has struck again.
jokes.punchline: Not only does she believe she killed him, she adds a size-based escalation — her curse must be 'getting stronger' to kill someone of Ugly Naked Guy's substantial mass.
jokes.explanation: The 'getting stronger, to bring down something that big' extension is brilliant — it turns a fat joke into a supernatural power scaling gag. Phoebe's body horror logic is perfectly in character: of course a more powerful curse needs a bigger victim. Dark, specific, and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ben, you look exhausted. What have you been doing all day?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Nothing, Dad. Just playing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, you must be doing something. Have you been bench pressing? Training for a marathon? Climbing Everest?

jokes.text: Maybe he's just taking a nap. / I'm telling you, he hasn't moved since this morning. / We should call somebody. / And tell them what? The naked guy we stare at isn't moving?
jokes.setup: The gang debates whether to call for help regarding the apparently motionless Ugly Naked Guy.
jokes.punchline: The logical problem of explaining the situation to authorities — 'the naked guy we stare at' — exposes their voyeuristic habit as absurd and indefensible.
jokes.explanation: 'The naked guy we stare at isn't moving?' perfectly captures the friends' complicity in their voyeuristic relationship with Ugly Naked Guy. The joke turns on them — the very act of calling for help would require admitting what they've been doing. Sharp self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I was just... demonstrating explosion sounds. For a play. A very loud play.

jokes.text: We've got to find out if he's alive. / How are we gonna do that? There's no way. / Well, there is one way. His window's open. I say... we poke him.
jokes.setup: The gang establishes they can't call authorities and there's 'no way' to check on Ugly Naked Guy.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, there is one way... we poke him.' — delivered as if it's the obvious, logical solution to the problem.
jokes.explanation: The episode title joke delivered as a perfectly confident solution. The pause before 'we poke him' and the matter-of-fact delivery are essential. The absurdity of poking a potentially dead man from across the street via a chopstick device is the episode's central comedic premise and this is its clean articulation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so glad that's over. I was terrified the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Let me just check... nobody died, right?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Not me, not the dentist, not anyone in this building?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Good, good. We're all still alive. That's the important thing.

jokes.text: You know how we save all those chopsticks... for no reason when we get Chinese food? Well, now we got a reason. / What? / We're fashioning a very long poking device.
jokes.setup: Ross reveals the plan to poke Ugly Naked Guy from across the street.
jokes.punchline: The mundane habit of saving chopsticks — acknowledged as purposeless — is suddenly given cosmic justification: they will build a giant poking device.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The pivot from universal habit (saving chopsticks 'for no reason') to this specific absurd justification is inspired. 'Well, now we got a reason' followed by 'We're fashioning a very long poking device' has a rhythm that's both pompous and ridiculous. 'Fashioning' is a perfect word choice — it makes the endeavor sound artisanal and serious. Strong originality. Near the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, the curse is finally over! I'm so happy!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's great, Phoebe. Hey, have you seen Chandler? He was supposed to meet us here twenty minutes ago.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh no.

jokes.text: It serves me right for buying that 12-pack of condoms. And now I can't even return them, because she choked on the receipt!
jokes.setup: Chandler is processing the Janice situation with Ross — he was optimistic about their relationship.
jokes.punchline: His regrets land on two specific, absurd details: (1) he bought a 12-pack of condoms in romantic optimism, and (2) he can't return them because the receipt was used as Janice's hyperventilation bag.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the stronger Chandler lines in the series. Two callbacks converge perfectly: the receipt used as a hyperventilation bag and the optimistic condom purchase. The specific '12-pack' (not just 'condoms' — a 12-pack implies romantic confidence and planning) is beautiful character writing. The logic chain (bought condoms optimistically → can't return them → because she choked on the receipt) is Rube Goldberg-style comedy engineering. Approaches the 8.0 anchor comfortably and arguably surpasses it in character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ugly Naked Guy is dead!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I guess he'll always be remembered as a legend. I mean, think about it — when he goes, half the building goes with him.

jokes.text: You know? What would you do?
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Joey what he would do if in Chandler's situation with Janice
jokes.punchline: Joey's very long pause before answering — the silence itself being funny because it implies Joey is either profoundly unqualified to give relationship advice or genuinely conflicted
jokes.explanation: A reaction beat that relies on performance more than writing — the comedy is in Joey's hesitation, implying he knows something hard is coming. Functional transitional moment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, you want to call the authorities? That's not creepy at all. I mean, it's not like we're talking about installing cameras in people's homes and tracking their every move without their knowledge or consent.

jokes.text: Are you sure it's a new bump? No offense, but I've always thought of Ben as a fairly bumpy-headed child.
jokes.setup: Monica is worried about the bump on Ben's head. Rachel tries to provide cover by questioning whether it's new.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'no offense' before insulting a baby's head shape, and her confident assertion that Ben has always been bumpy-headed, is a wonderfully callous observation.
jokes.explanation: 'No offense, but I've always thought of Ben as a fairly bumpy-headed child' is a great line. The 'no offense' before critiquing an infant's skull is a perfectly Rachel-ian move. The word 'fairly' does a lot of work — it implies she's being measured and generous about Ben's bumpiness. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Finally finding a use for pointlessly saved chopsticks

jokes.text: I did! I watched! I watched! I watched Monica bang his head against that thing!
jokes.setup: Ross questions whether they were watching Ben properly. Rachel, under pressure, breaks.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's insistence that she WAS watching — 'I watched Monica bang his head' — accidentally and completely incriminates Monica in trying to defend herself.
jokes.explanation: Great comedic structure — Rachel's defense of her own vigilance ('I watched! I watched!') inadvertently becomes a full confession implicating Monica. The repetition of 'I watched' builds to the perfect self-betrayal. Classic comedic payoff to the babysitting arc.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I bought a bulk pack of condoms in 1987. That's why I haven't had a relationship since.

jokes.text: Did you notice anything weird about Ben today? / No, why? / I was just playing with him, and we were doing the 'Alphabet Song'... which he used to be good at. Suddenly, he's leaving out E and F. It's like they just, I don't know, fell out of his head.
jokes.setup: Ross casually mentions he was playing alphabet song with Ben.
jokes.punchline: Ben is now skipping E and F in the alphabet — Monica's guilt and the audience's horror at the implication (brain damage?) creates dark comedy.
jokes.explanation: The 'fell out of his head' phrase is brilliant and horrifying — it perfectly describes what a bump-related cognitive gap might feel like from a child's perspective. The dark implication (Monica caused cognitive damage) is played for cringe-comedy. 'Which he used to be good at' is a great understated qualifier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The condoms are too big! I can't return them because the cashier knows my face now.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So go to a different store.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't! I hyperventilated in front of the pharmacist. He thinks I'm unstable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, that was three weeks ago.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Exactly! He'll remember the crazy guy who passed out by the Chapstick.

jokes.text: And also, he's walking... kind of funny. It's like his left leg is moving a lot faster than his right leg.
jokes.setup: Ross is casually listing cognitive and physical changes in Ben since the babysitting session.
jokes.punchline: Now Ben also has a gait problem — walking with uneven leg speeds, again suggesting possible neurological damage from the head bump.
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating babysitting horror arc. The specificity of 'his left leg is moving a lot faster than his right leg' creates a vivid, dark comic image. The escalation from alphabet gaps to uneven gait is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why is there a bump on Ben's head?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, he was already bumpy-headed.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! I wrecked your baby! / I hope it's still funny when you're in hell.
jokes.setup: Monica can no longer maintain the fiction — convinced by Ross's 'symptoms' that she has genuinely damaged Ben.
jokes.punchline: Monica's full confession ('I wrecked your baby!') and Ross's scorching response ('I hope it's still funny when you're in hell') is the cringe comedy peak of this arc.
jokes.explanation: 'I wrecked your baby' is an endearingly specific confession — not 'I hurt Ben' but 'I wrecked your baby' as if he's a car. Ross's 'I hope it's still funny when you're in hell' is a quotable, perfectly calibrated expression of sibling rage. Both lines are character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I am an excellent babysitter. I watch Emma like a hawk.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A hawk that fell asleep during your shift last Tuesday.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I did not fall asleep! And how would you even know that? You weren't there!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because I came home and found Emma teaching the cat to use the toilet.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She's a very smart baby!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you weren't supposed to tell me about that either.

jokes.text: I hope it's still funny when you're in hell.
jokes.setup: Monica confesses she's wrecked the baby; Ross's reaction is presumably being played
jokes.punchline: Ross's damnation of Monica to hell delivered with flat affect — implying he's been watching all along and found it funny but now feels the need to assert parental outrage
jokes.explanation: 'I hope it's still funny when you're in hell' is a good Ross line — dryly threatening while also implicitly admitting he finds it funny. The delivery-specific nature of this joke limits its craft score slightly, but it's a sharp line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, he's brain damaged!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: He's not brain damaged.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, he's wrecked!

jokes.text: You jerk! You know how much I love that kid! / Monica bang! Monica bang!
jokes.setup: Monica protests her love for Ben in the middle of being accused of injuring him.
jokes.punchline: Ben chimes in with 'Monica bang! Monica bang!' — an impeccably timed contribution that completely undermines Monica's defense.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Monica's declaration of love for Ben is immediately demolished by Ben himself repeating 'Monica bang' as if in accusation. A baby functioning as witness for the prosecution is comedy gold. The structure is flawless — Monica protests, Ben indicts. Running gag reaches its comedic peak here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You laugh now, but when you're all in hell, don't come crying to me!

jokes.text: I'll get the hat.
jokes.setup: The babysitting cover-up is fully exposed. The damage is done.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's resigned 'I'll get the hat' — reverting to the useless original cover plan despite it being pointless now — is a perfect button.
jokes.explanation: Three words. One of the episode's cleverest single-line jokes. The cover is blown, Ben has fully testified against Monica, and Rachel's response is to fall back on the useless hat scheme. It's funny because it's completely pointless and because Rachel's coping mechanism is to keep doing something rather than face consequences. Economy is essentially perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I mean, you know, it's like... love is when you can't explain it, you just feel it. Like trying to understand Lionel Richie lyrics.

jokes.text: The way I feel about you... it's like I finally understand what Lionel Richie's been singing about.
jokes.setup: Chandler is giving Janice an emotional farewell speech, trying to express deep romantic feeling.
jokes.punchline: He reaches for poetic expression and lands on... Lionel Richie. The specific choice of Lionel Richie as the poet laureate of his deepest feelings is both touching and ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Chandler reaching for Lionel Richie in a moment of genuine heartbreak is funny precisely because it's sincere — he truly means this as the highest possible praise. The specificity of Richie (Hello? All Night Long? Easy?) makes it funnier than a generic music reference would be. Good character integration for Chandler's awkward romantic earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: You deserve someone's whole heart.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'll settle for three-quarters. I mean, everybody's got stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I could live with two-thirds of a heart. That's... that's more than half.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? I'll take a ventricle. Just... just one ventricle.

jokes.text: Then don't leave me. / What? / Forget what I said. I was babbling. Pick me!
jokes.setup: Chandler nobly tells Janice to go back to her husband. She seems moved.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately reverses himself — 'Forget what I said. I was babbling. Pick me!' — the noble sacrifice lasting approximately three seconds.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler self-sabotage. The noble romantic gesture immediately undermined by his own neediness is perfectly in character. 'I was babbling. Pick me!' has the right desperate energy. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! You can't leave!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because... because you forgot your shoe!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I'm wearing both my shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you're gonna need a third one!

jokes.text: No, you were right! I gotta give my marriage another chance. / No, you don't! I say, you have to give your divorce another chance!
jokes.setup: Chandler has just recanted his noble speech and begged Janice to stay; Janice invokes his original argument
jokes.punchline: Chandler's desperate counter — 'give your divorce another chance!' — is a wonderful absurdist inversion of the usual 'give it another chance' rhetoric
jokes.explanation: 'Give your divorce another chance' is a highly quotable, original inversion. The phrase takes the cliché of 'give it another chance' and applies it to the thing that would benefit Chandler — the divorce. It works as absurdist desperation and as Chandler's signature move of deflecting pain into a quip. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, I know you're upset about Janice, but that shirt is hideous.

jokes.text: No, you were right! I gotta give my marriage another chance. / No, you don't! I say, you have to give your divorce another chance!
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to walk back his noble advice. Janice takes it seriously and decides to recommit to her marriage.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reframes 'give your marriage another chance' as 'give your divorce another chance' — a grammatically parallel but logically opposite instruction delivered in panic.
jokes.explanation: 'Give your divorce another chance' is a clever inversion of the romantic cliché. The panic behind it and the grammatical mirroring of the original phrase give it structure. Good economy. Character-appropriate desperation from Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's what she said!

jokes.text: Sweetie, you should not have to settle for just half my heart. / I'll settle for half your heart. I'll settle for a quarter. / I'll settle for a little, tiny... A ventricle.
jokes.setup: Janice makes a noble point that Chandler's heart is divided. He tries to reassure her.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's desperate de-escalation of his romantic requirements — from half, to a quarter, to 'a ventricle' — is a comedic countdown of self-worth.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. The countdown from 'half' to 'quarter' to 'a ventricle' is beautifully structured — each step down is funnier, and 'ventricle' as the terminal anatomical unit is both specific and sad. It perfectly captures Chandler's self-deprecating desperation in a way no other character could deliver. Approaches the 8.0 anchor. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's what she said!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey! Oh my God, you know what? You need to grow up!

jokes.text: You can't leave! I have your shoe!
jokes.setup: Janice says goodbye and begins to leave. Chandler desperately tries to stop her.
jokes.punchline: In a moment of romantic desperation, Chandler's final argument is that he has her shoe — the most mundane possible hostage situation.
jokes.explanation: Six words, maximum impact. The absurdity of 'I have your shoe!' as a last-ditch romantic gambit is perfectly Chandler — it's desperate, pathetic, and somehow endearing. Economy is near-perfect. The image of him holding a single shoe while his heart breaks is classic physical comedy implied through dialogue. Quotable and memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: All right, I'm going in. If I don't come back, tell my mother I love her.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you're just poking him with a stick.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, but what if he wakes up angry? What if he comes after me? I could lose a limb, man. Do you know how much that would affect my acting career?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, it might improve it.

jokes.text: Rachel has those in burgundy. [looking at Janice's departing shoes]
jokes.setup: Janice has just left, taking the shoe back. The emotional scene ends.
jokes.punchline: Joey's contribution to the devastating breakup scene is to note that Rachel has those shoes in burgundy. Completely irrelevant, completely Joey.
jokes.explanation: Five words that are perfectly Joey. In the wake of Chandler's heartbreak, Joey's mind goes to fashion inventory. The tonal deflation from romantic tragedy to shoe color is enormous, and Joey's total obliviousness is the joke. 'Burgundy' specifically is funnier than any other color would be. High character integration score — this joke is only possible because it's Joey. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We haven't stopped poking him.

jokes.text: Remember, something this big and long will be very difficult to maneuver. / Fortunately, I have experience in that area.
jokes.setup: The gang prepares to deploy the giant chopstick poking device across the street.
jokes.punchline: Ross's technical warning about maneuvering the large device is instantly and deliberately misread by Joey as a sexual innuendo.
jokes.explanation: A fairly standard innuendo joke — 'big and long' + 'I have experience in that area.' The setup is obvious and the punchline entirely predictable. Joey's sexual self-confidence is on-brand but this is one of the lazier jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: What are you, 12 today? Can we please focus here? A naked man's life hangs in the balance.
jokes.setup: Joey makes the 'big and long' innuendo. Monica is exasperated.
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'what are you, 12?' is followed immediately by the absurd gravity of 'a naked man's life hangs in the balance' — earnest urgency about a possibly dead voyeurism subject.
jokes.explanation: 'A naked man's life hangs in the balance' is a funny sentence to say earnestly. Monica's combination of mature exasperation and complete commitment to the absurd mission is solid character comedy. The 'what are you, 12?' straight-man line before it sets it up well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could he BE any farther away?

jokes.text: I'm telling you, he's dead. What we're about to have here is a dead, fat guy on a stick!
jokes.setup: The group is about to attempt to poke Ugly Naked Guy to check if he's alive.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe articulates the worst-case scenario with vivid specificity: 'a dead, fat guy on a stick' — framing the poking as potential shish-kebab of a corpse.
jokes.explanation: 'A dead, fat guy on a stick' is a darkly vivid image delivered with Phoebe's characteristic blunt earnestness. The horror of accidentally impaling a dead man with chopsticks is rendered comically specific. Strong economy and originality within the dark humor register.

jokes.text: All right, ladies and gentlemen, let's poke. / Steady. / Okay, a little higher. / Careful of the angle. / Okay, okay. We're approaching the window. / Thread the needle. Thread the needle.
jokes.setup: The group begins deploying the giant chopstick device toward Ugly Naked Guy's apartment window.
jokes.punchline: The whole sequence is played with the gravity and precision of a NASA mission — 'ladies and gentlemen, let's poke,' 'thread the needle' — treating naked-man-poking as a serious technical operation.
jokes.explanation: The comedic engine here is the contrast between the technical precision of the language and the absurdity of the activity. 'Thread the needle' applied to poking a naked man through a window with taped chopsticks is gloriously ridiculous. The escalating mission-control language builds well.

jokes.text: He's alive! He's alive! / And yet we're still poking him.
jokes.setup: The chopstick poke works — Ugly Naked Guy reacts, confirming he's alive. Mission accomplished.
jokes.punchline: Despite the confirmed alive status, they continue poking him anyway. The mission objective is achieved but the poking continues reflexively.
jokes.explanation: 'And yet we're still poking him' — six words, perfect comic deflation. The observation that they're continuing the poke after the crisis is resolved is a great meta-observation. Economy is excellent and the dry delivery is the joke.

jokes.text: Okay, retract the device! Retract the device! / He does not look happy. / Now he's showing us his poking device. / Hey, that's never gonna make it all the way over here, buddy!
jokes.setup: Ugly Naked Guy wakes up angry from being poked. He apparently retaliates.
jokes.punchline: Ugly Naked Guy's 'poking device' — implied to be his genitals — is brandished in retaliation, and Joey confidently dismisses its reach.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke is a well-constructed escalation: they poke him, he shows his 'poking device,' and Joey delivers the dismissive callback to scale. 'That's never gonna make it all the way over here, buddy!' is Joey's masculine confidence applied to a surreal situation. The wordplay on 'poking device' is the episode's final pun and it lands well as a button. Strong structure.

jokes.text: Hey, that's never gonna make it all the way over here, buddy!
jokes.setup: UNG is apparently brandishing himself in the window; Joey responds
jokes.punchline: Joey's competitive trash-talk about UNG's anatomy — treating it as a distance/capability challenge
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and a very strong one. Joey turning this into a distance competition — implying his own anatomy would cover it while UNG's won't — is both juvenile and perfectly character-specific. The confidence of the delivery is everything. Good closer for the episode.

tmdb_overview: When Phoebe believes she's killed the ugly naked guy across the street from Rachel and Monica, Joey constructs a long poking device. Joey and Monica catch Janice kissing her ex-husband; Chandler confronts Janice.
insight: Giant poking device escalates from absurd premise to 64 jokes in 22 minutes, carrying a middling episode.
